The House of Plantagenet. Named for the yellow broom flowers worn in the hat of their founder Geoffrey of Anjou, the Plantagenets ruled England from 1154 to 1485, the longest-reigning English royal house. They produced strong medieval warrior-kings and gave England the Magna Carta, common law traditions, and Parliament itself.

Henry II founded the dynasty in 1154. Descended from Norman conquerors, the Plantagenets controlled England and large territories in France as the Angevin Empire. King John was forced by rebellious barons to seal the Magna Carta in 1215, a foundational document limiting royal power and establishing the rule of law. King Henry III and his son Edward I expanded English law, centralized governance, and conquered Wales. Edward I also campaigned in Scotland, claiming overlordship.

Richard the Lionheart reigned from 1189 to 1199 as a legendary Crusader king, though he rarely set foot in England during his reign and bankrupted the realm. The Plantagenets presided over the birth of Parliament as an institution where the crown consulted with the nobility and common representatives on taxation and law.

Later, the dynasty fragmented into rival factions. The House of York flew the white rose and the House of Lancaster the red rose, and they fought the Wars of the Roses from 1455 to 1487. Richard III, the last Plantagenet king, reigned from 1483 to 1485 before he was killed at Bosworth Field, ending the dynasty and making way for the House of Tudor.
